title: Transformers Provably Learn Algorithmic Solutions for Graph Connectivity, But Only with the Right Data
one_liner: Show that a transformer can learn the exact graph-connectivity algorithm, but only when the training graphs mostly fit the depth limit of the model.
lead: A graph-connectivity task asks a simple question: given two nodes, is there any path between them? Standard training of a transformer (a layered sequence model that repeatedly mixes information across positions) often fails to learn the exact rule and instead learns shortcuts that work only on the training range. This paper explains why. It proves that a simplified transformer can compute connectivity by repeatedly expanding reachability, but only up to a graph diameter limit set by the number of layers. It then shows that training data beyond that limit pushes learning toward a degree-based shortcut instead of the exact algorithm.

problem.h2: Why algorithm learning and shortcut learning get mixed together
paras: To solve connectivity exactly, a model must determine whether reachability can be propagated through several hops. That requires a computation whose depth grows with graph diameter, because information from one node must travel through intermediate nodes before the answer is known.

A transformer can instead learn a shortcut. For many training data patterns, connected node pairs correlate with simple local signals such as high degree or short paths. Those signals are easier to pick up early in training. If the training set contains many graphs whose diameters exceed the model's layer capacity, the exact algorithm cannot fit them anyway, so optimization has an incentive to settle on the cheaper shortcut because the shortcut still lowers loss on those impossible cases.

callout.b: The paper's claim in one sentence.
callout.html: The model can learn the real connectivity procedure, but the training data must mostly stay inside the diameter range that the model depth can represent.

panels.title: 1. Input is a graph plus a queried node pair
panels.viz_args: The model must answer whether the two marked nodes lie in the same connected component.
panels.caption: The task depends on multi-hop reachability, not on one local edge.

panels.title: 2. Exact solution needs repeated propagation
panels.caption: Each layer can spread information only a limited distance, so depth sets the reachable diameter.

panels.title: 3. Out-of-capacity graphs distort training
panels.viz_args: When many graphs exceed the depth limit, the model cannot fit them with the exact rule.
panels.caption: Optimization then favors any local pattern that reduces loss quickly.

panels.title: 4. Within-capacity data supports algorithm learning
panels.caption: When most examples fit the depth budget, the exact computation becomes the easiest good solution.

panels.title: 5. Data choice decides what gets learned
panels.caption: The same model class can learn a real algorithm or a brittle shortcut depending on the graph data pattern.

steps.text: Study the disentangled architecture because it is simple enough for proofs but still captures the key message-passing behavior of the full model.
Show that an L-layer model can propagate connectivity information across graph diameters up to 3 to the power L.
Relate the layer updates to repeated multiplication of the adjacency matrix, which builds longer and longer reachability paths.
Analyze which signal dominates training when the data mixes easy within-capacity graphs and impossible beyond-capacity graphs.

steps.b: Verify the lesson on standard transformers
steps.text: Train ordinary transformers on restricted and unrestricted graph sets to confirm that the same data-capacity effect appears in practice.

paras: The paper changes the explanation for transformer failure on algorithmic tasks. The issue is not only that the architecture lacks the right operation. The issue is also that the training set can reward a shortcut more strongly than the exact algorithm when too many examples exceed model capacity.
object.object: the explanation of when transformers learn exact graph algorithms

hidden.name: the fraction of training graphs that fit the model's depth budget
paras: The key quantity is the share of graphs whose diameters are small enough for the model to solve exactly. If that share is high, the loss can be reduced by learning the true propagation rule, because the rule succeeds on many examples and extends cleanly to nearby cases.

If that share is low, the exact rule cannot explain much of the dataset. Then early training updates favor local hints such as node degree, since those hints improve training loss on many examples even though they do not encode connectivity itself.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark the conditions that strengthen the training signal for the exact connectivity procedure instead of the degree-based shortcut.

reads.html: What matters most is how often the training set asks the model to solve cases it can actually represent with its available layers.
Within-capacity examples drive the training updates toward adjacency-power computation, because those examples reward repeated reachability propagation that the network depth can realize.

mechanism.h2: Why the training data determines whether the model learns the algorithm
paras: In the proved construction, each layer expands the set of nodes known to be reachable. After one layer, the model can combine local edge information. After more layers, that information has passed through intermediate nodes, so the model can represent longer paths because each added layer performs one more reachability expansion. The result is a bounded but exact procedure for connectivity.

Training does not automatically discover that procedure. The optimizer follows whichever pattern gives the clearest loss reduction first. On within-capacity graphs, the exact propagation rule explains the labels, so its signal accumulates across batches. On beyond-capacity graphs, the rule cannot finish the job, so the training updates from those examples push toward easier local statistics that partially correlate with the labels.

That is why restricting the training set helps. The restriction does not add new compute or new modules. It changes the optimization target so the exact rule is rewarded often enough to become the dominant learned computation.

stages.s: Each layer propagates reachability information one expansion step
Depth limit caps the diameter the model can solve exactly
Training updates come mostly from within-capacity or beyond-capacity cases
Dominant training signal selects either the exact rule or a shortcut
Generalizable connectivity behavior only when exact-rule training updates dominate

math.words: Connectivity can be computed by repeatedly expanding which nodes are reachable from the source. One matrix multiplication adds another hop of reachability information.
symbols: the adjacency matrix of the graph
the indicator of which nodes are reachable after t propagation steps
the updated reachable-node indicator after one more propagation step

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Start from one source node, so only that node is marked reachable at step 0.
After one multiplication by the adjacency matrix, every direct neighbor becomes marked reachable.
After the next multiplication, neighbors of those neighbors become reachable as well.
Repeating this process long enough reveals whether the target node is in the same connected component.

math.note: The proof shows that the layer stack can emulate this repeated update up to a diameter bound determined by model depth.

charts.title: Training with many beyond-capacity graphs
charts.note: The model still fits part of the dataset, but it does so with local cues because many examples cannot be solved exactly at the available depth.

charts.title: Training restricted to within-capacity graphs
charts.note: Restricting the diameter range changes what the training updates reward, so the exact propagation rule becomes the stable solution.

items.b: Too much restricted data can narrow the task.
items.html: If the training set covers only very easy graphs, the model may still fail on larger but in-capacity cases because it never learned the full range of intermediate path structures.

items.b: The proof applies to a simplified architecture first.
items.html: Standard transformers include additional interactions, so the exact constructive proof does not transfer line by line even though the data-capacity lesson appears in experiments on the larger architecture.

items.b: Shortcut cues depend on the data generator.
items.html: If a benchmark accidentally makes degree or other local statistics strongly predictive, the model may keep using them unless the dataset is designed to break those correlations.

Match the graph-diameter range to model depth, keep enough variety inside that range, and test on data patterns that break local shortcuts because that exposes whether the model learned the exact rule.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate random graphs and ask whether marked node pairs are connected. Train one transformer on graphs whose diameters mostly fit the chosen layer depth and a second transformer on a mixed set that includes many larger-diameter graphs.

Then evaluate both on graphs that preserve the same connectivity rule but vary node counts and degree patterns. The demo should show that the restricted-data model keeps working when local shortcuts break, because its training updates favored repeated reachability propagation instead of degree correlation.
demo.metric_eq: generalization_gap = accuracy_in_range - accuracy_out_of_range ; shortcut_gap = accuracy_shortcut_friendly - accuracy_shortcut_broken
demo.closing: The important result is not only final accuracy. It is which computation the model learned, revealed by whether performance survives when the shortcut cues disappear.
